sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E3733. This annotation uses only the supplied transcript; cited research and historical claims were not independently verified. Transcription errors, missing speaker labels, and events containing speaker changes limit attribution. U marks inseparably mixed events or genuinely uncertain turns. No edited teaser replay was identifiable.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: when good people do bad things it's religion
candidates.explanation: Krauss adopts Weinberg's maxim as his concluding inference, rather than merely reporting it. The witch-burning account supplies a proposed religious mechanism in one case (E1435–1462), but no reason establishes religion as the general explanation for good people's wrongdoing. Nothing makes contrary examples automatically confirm the maxim.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: I don't need some guy to say well the Inquisition was distorted Christianity
candidates.explanation: Krauss rejects an anticipated historical qualification before hearing it, potentially shielding his attribution of inquisitorial harms to Christianity (E1505–1523). However, he explicitly distinguishes observable conduct from doctrinal ideals (E1511–1516). The text leaves uncertain whether he excludes relevant causal evidence regardless of merits or rejects an appeal that misconduct misrepresents Christianity.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: you're only damaging Humanity by trying to reduce Christianity
candidates.explanation: Jones urges critics to let Christianity grow uninhibited, treating successful criticism as socially damaging. His earlier welfare and fertility arguments supply reasons for concern, but do not establish that every reduction is harmful. E2148–2150 ties the injunction to evidence; E3037–3057 later allows adverse evidence to count against Christianity.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: I don't believe anything I follow the evidence
candidates.explanation: The affirmation answers a challenge about whether contrary scientific findings should reverse moral judgments without clearly identifying the normative standard connecting evidence to obligation. It also summarizes Krauss's previously explained fallibilism (E703–724). His later necessary-but-not-sufficient qualification (E2957–2971) makes an interpretation as complete substitution uncertain; no objection-proof mechanism appears.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: you don't need to go in a look in a book to look around you
candidates.explanation: Asked for comparative studies, Krauss offers observation of present prosperity; this leaves its comparative attribution to secularism unresolved. His historical argument and Pinker reference provide reasons elsewhere (E1197–1219). The wording potentially excludes relevant studies, but his later agreement to read Jones's references (E3276–3279) prevents confidently treating that exclusion as unconditional.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: it would definitely factor into that going well maybe this isn't of God
contrasts.explanation: Jones explicitly permits harmful social results to count against his belief, while explaining that historical and resurrection evidence also matter. Considering several grounds is a qualified evidential position, not automatic protection against criticism.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: it's a necessary but not sufficient condition
contrasts.explanation: Krauss explains that understanding consequences informs action while conceding that empirical facts alone may not establish moral obligations. This qualifies earlier broad appeals to science and supplies a reason for its relevance.
